column2: Prologue
Darkness in the Torrent of Rain
A Dark Rainy Night
But Chu Zihang did not want to forget, because he was the only person in the world who still remembered that man. If he forgot too, it would be as though the man had never existed.
The man had once said that if he died one day, only one thing in the world could prove he had existed: Chu Zihang, who carried half his blood.
Chu Zihang stood at the window in a daze.
Rain rattled against the glass. The playing field was a blur of white.

The afternoon had been bright and sunny, but as the dismissal bell rang, leaden clouds swept in from the southeast and the sky darkened within minutes. Then thunder exploded, and millions upon millions of tons of water fell on the earth as though a reservoir in the sky had opened its gates.

Tire tracks crisscrossed the soccer field, its turf churned to pieces. Private cars were normally forbidden on campus, but in such terrible weather the parents worried about their children getting wet. Several forced the iron gates open, and all the cars swarmed inside. Half an hour ago the field had been as crowded as a market: cars parked every which way, hazard lights flashing a confusion of yellow, everyone leaning on their horns and shouting their children’s names. In the downpour, students unable to find their families’ cars wandered around like headless flies.
Now everyone had been collected. The classrooms and playing field were empty, and the sky-blue flag of Shilan High School fluttered wildly in the storm.
Like the dispersal of a crowd when the music ends.
He was alone in the classroom, beneath pale lights, while outside was as dark as midnight. On a day like this, people should go home early.
He took out his phone, dialed, switched on the speaker, and set it on the desk, watching it in silence.

After several rings, the call connected. “Zihang, it’s raining where you are too, isn’t it? Oh, Mom’s shopping at Jiuguang Department Store with her friends. It’s pouring here, and we can’t get a cab. We’re having coffee and waiting for the rain to let up. Get yourself a taxi home, or call your dad and ask him to send a car. Be good, Zihang. Mommy sends you a kiss.” A crisp kissing sound came through the phone, and she hung up.
Chu Zihang put away his phone. He hadn’t said a single word, nor had he planned to. He had called only to let his mother know he was all right, so she wouldn’t worry and could keep enjoying herself.
Adults could be foolish sometimes. When a child reached out to comfort one, she thought he was asking for food.

There were no taxis outside. In rain this heavy, drivers didn’t want the business and had gone home early. If there were no cars at Jiuguang, it was the same at school, but his mother wouldn’t think of that. His grandmother said his mother was an innocent little girl, without a care in the world. Chu Zihang didn’t want to call “Dad” either. “Dad” was a very busy man who wouldn’t remember the small matter of sending a car for his stepson on a rainy day. But if reminded, he would certainly send a driver. “Dad” was a fine, responsible, well-mannered man who loved his beautiful wife, a former dancer, and treated her son well for her sake. He often said, “Zihang, if you need anything, just say so. I’m your father, and I’ll fulfill my responsibilities to you.”
Having a wealthy “Dad” who wanted to fulfill his responsibilities sounded rather good.
But Chu Zihang didn’t think he needed it.
The classroom door stood open. Cold wind and fine rain blew in, chilling him to the bone. Chu Zihang pulled his jacket tighter, stuck his hands in his pockets, and resumed staring into space.

“Chu Zihang? Let’s go together. The rain won’t stop—the forecast says it’s a typhoon, and the weather bureau issued a warning!” A girl peeked in. Her long hair fell clean and straight, with a silver Hello Kitty clip at the end. Her delicate face was slightly flushed, and she lowered her eyes, too shy to meet his gaze.
“You don’t know me? I’m Liu Miaomiao...” Receiving no answer, her voice grew softer and softer, like a mosquito’s hum.

Actually, Chu Zihang did know Liu Miaomiao. A year below him, she was famous at Shilan High. She had passed the tenth-grade piano examination in her second year of middle school and played a solo at every annual celebration. Several boys in his class competed for her attention in secret; he could hardly have avoided knowing who she was.
“I’m on cleaning duty today. I’ll leave in a while.” Chu Zihang nodded politely.
“Oh... then I’ll go first.” Liu Miaomiao spoke softly and withdrew her head.

Through the window, Chu Zihang watched her family’s driver open an enormous black umbrella over her. She took off her strappy sandals, and the driver crouched to help her into rain boots. Sheltering under the umbrella, she picked her way toward a black BMW whose “angel eye” headlights shone through the rain.
“Hey! Liu Miaomiao! Give me a ride!” a younger boy shouted from under the eaves.
“Walk, Lu Mingfei! My house isn’t in the same direction as yours!” Liu Miaomiao didn’t turn around.

Actually, Chu Zihang’s home wasn’t in the same direction as Liu Miaomiao’s either. His was in Peacock Residence in the east of the city, hers in California Sunshine in the west, opposite directions altogether. Yet she had offered him a ride.

The younger boy squatted under the eaves and watched the BMW glide silently into the rain. Its taillights flashed, its engine roared, and it was gone. He stood, head drooping to one side, and walked slowly along the eaves. Watching his retreating figure, Chu Zihang suddenly thought he might give him a ride. But the boy ducked his head, wrapped his coat over it, and darted into the rain like a stray dog. He ran so fast that before Chu Zihang could call out, he had splashed away into the distance.

Zigzag lightning flickered in the clouds, and thunder burst overhead. The rain grew heavier. Liu Miaomiao was right: this was no ordinary rain, but a typhoon. Suddenly Chu Zihang very much wanted someone to pick him up. Otherwise he would have to splash through the cold rain like that younger boy. He took out his phone and typed: “It’s raining hard. Can you come pick me up?” He read it over silently, made sure the tone was right, and sent it.
For the next several dozen seconds he counted his heartbeats. Thump-thump... thump-thump... thump-thump...
“Sure, sure, no problem! Wait at school. I’ll be there in a bit!” The reply came. That person always sounded so cheerful.

Chu Zihang deleted both messages; it would be awkward if “Dad” saw them. He picked up the bucket at his feet and threw all the water onto the blackboard. Water streamed down as he seized an eraser and scrubbed hard.
On his third pass, a low horn sounded outside. He turned. Through the rain, xenon headlights cast two dazzling beams that made him squint.
It was a pure black sedan. In a triangular frame on its hood, two overlapping M’s formed a mountain. A Maybach 62.
Maybach was Mercedes-Benz’s top marque, apparently several times more expensive than “Dad’s” Mercedes S500. Chu Zihang wasn’t much interested in cars. The man inside had boasted all this to him.

The wipers swung back and forth like a deranged metronome, clearing layer after layer of rain from the windshield. The middle-aged man inside waved to Chu Zihang, his face blooming with a smile. Chu Zihang couldn’t understand why he always looked so happy, as if nothing ever troubled him. Shouldering the Hermès bag “Dad” had bought him in London, Chu Zihang locked the classroom, checked the door, and walked to the edge of the eaves. He hesitated a moment before the downpour. The man hurried out, opened a huge black umbrella, and came to meet him, as attentive as Liu Miaomiao’s driver. Chu Zihang didn’t look at him. He pushed the umbrella aside, walked through the rain to the car, opened the rear door himself, and climbed in.

His attempt at ingratiation unanswered, the man paused, then climbed back into the driver’s seat. He closed the umbrella and passed it to Chu Zihang in the back. “Stick it in the door. There’s a hole just for umbrellas.”
“I know. You told me.” Chu Zihang put it away and turned to the window. “Let’s go.”
“Your clothes are wet, right? Want me to turn on the rear-seat heating? Once you try it, you’ll know—comfortable as hell!” The man began boasting about his car again.
“No need. I’ll change at home.”
“Oh, okay.” The man cleared his throat and spoke to the center console. “Start!”

The screen lit up, a cold blue light flashed across the dashboard, and the savage 5.5-liter turbocharged V12 began its self-check. Not a vibration could be felt inside; even the engine’s deep growl was shut out.
“A nine-million-yuan car, no key. Only three voices in the world can start it: mine, my boss’s, and guess whose?” The man looked immensely pleased.
“Not interested.” Chu Zihang’s face was expressionless.

Again the man’s warmth met a cold shoulder, but he wasn’t discouraged. He shifted and accelerated briskly. The Maybach roared forward, sweeping in a great arc across the field and cutting through the rain like a blade as it drove through Shilan High’s gate. The guard stood ramrod straight in his booth, chest and belly thrust out in respect for the luxury car and the wealth it represented.

Chu Zihang couldn’t see what there was to respect. On a rainy day like this, all you needed was a car to pick you up and someone who remembered to come. Whether it was a Maybach, a Mercedes S500, or a QQ made no difference.
“Such heavy rain, and your mother didn’t think to pick you up.”
“Lucky I didn’t get the car washed this morning. An eighty-yuan touchless wash would have been money down the drain.”

“That guard at your school wouldn’t let me drive in. I told him I was picking up my son, and he’d get soaked in rain like this if I couldn’t go in. Took no end of arguing. Finally I told him this car cost nine million, and nobody stops me driving into city hall, so why should Shilan High be so damned strict? He backed down right away. Ha ha!”
The man chattered on as he handled the wheel with a flourish.
Chu Zihang hadn’t answered him once since getting in. He turned on the radio; the announcer’s voice gave him more peace than the man’s.

“We now bring you an emergency typhoon warning and traffic update. According to the municipal weather station, Typhoon Dandelion, number 0407 this year, made landfall on the city’s southeastern coast this afternoon. Heavy rain and force-ten winds are expected. All organizations should take precautions. Due to the intense rainfall, provincial and national highways through the city will close in two hours. Winds are high on the elevated roads and visibility is below thirty meters. Drivers still on the road should take alternative routes.”

He looked out. Visibility really was terrible: beyond fifty meters everything dissolved into a white haze. The raindrops were so dense they seemed to smash one another apart in the air, falling as a spray of foam. The sky was black as ink; occasional bolts of lightning struck straight down. Few cars remained, all creeping carefully with headlights on. When two met, their drivers sounded their horns hard, like beasts encountering each other in a forest, baring their teeth and growling a warning.
Traffic slowed to a crawl, one car feeling its way behind another. Horns shrilled ahead like boiling kettles, and countless red brake lights pierced the rain. There seemed to be a jam.
“You want my V12 to crawl like a turtle?” the man muttered. He swung the wheel and forced his way into the emergency lane.

It was a beautiful cut, like a sharp blade slicing through water, severing the stream of traffic behind them. The driver of an Audi braked hard, locked wheels skidding across the road. Without braking, the Audi would have hit the Maybach from behind, and the Audi driver would have been entirely responsible. Repairing the Maybach would cost as much as an Audi. The braking opened a one-second gap in the traffic, and the man squeezed into it.
“Do you know how to fucking drive? Rushing to a funeral?”

The man winked proudly at Chu Zihang, ignoring the Audi driver’s shouted curses. The luxury car, more than six meters long, was like an iron catfish in his hands, flicking its tail at just the right moment and swimming freely through traffic. Who knew how many drivers rolled down their windows and cursed after he overtook them? A chorus of sharp horns followed. But there was little they could do: the car overtaking them was an ultraluxury vehicle with sports-car performance, and its driver was clearly skilled.
The man grinned broadly.

Chu Zihang couldn’t see what he was so happy about. Would it kill him to follow the traffic slowly? He simply had to show off his car and his tricks. He was a professional driver; of course he should be good at driving.
“Damn it, we’re really stuck!” the man swore.

Two cars had scraped each other ahead. Their drivers stood under umbrellas, spitting as they shouted. In weather like this, traffic police couldn’t arrive quickly, and each blamed the other. Dozens of cars were blocked. Several drivers got out and told the arguing men to move their vehicles, only for another argument to break out, with pushing and shoving. Everyone else pressed their horns impatiently.
Chu Zihang wanted to cover his ears. What a mess. The whole world was a mess.
“Are they idiots? What’s there to argue about over two lousy little cars? Insurance pays anyway,” the man grumbled. “I’ve got things to do after I drop off my son...”

He craned his neck and looked around, his gaze settling on a branch road in the rain. An entrance to the elevated highway, just a step away; its sign was hidden among a willow’s wildly thrashing branches. It was odd. The trapped cars should have poured onto an empty road, yet not a soul was there. Something stirred in Chu Zihang, a strange feeling that only they could see the road, or else everyone else knew it was impassable. His biology teacher had said animals had an instinct for finding their way: wild camels in the desert knew which paths were wrong and had no springs, and wouldn’t take them even if driven.
“That road should lead up to the elevated highway, though it’s probably closed now,” the man said, even as he pointed the car straight toward it.
Closer up, the sign read “Elevated Highway Entrance...” followed by its number. Chu Zihang looked, but a sheet of rain burst against the windshield at that moment, and he couldn’t make it out.
The Maybach climbed the ramp. The elevated road stretched ahead like a gray rainbow, disappearing into the white rain.
“What if it really is closed and we can’t get down?” Chu Zihang asked.
“If we can get up, we can get down.” The man wasn’t worried. “At worst I’ll offer the cop at the exit a cigarette.”

“The radio said the wind’s strong and visibility’s poor up here. It told drivers to take another route.” Chu Zihang was uneasy. He didn’t know how fast the wind outside was blowing, but it shrieked like a whistle.

“It’s fine.” The man patted the wheel. “What’s a little wind? Tiny cars have to worry about that. Know how much a Maybach 62 weighs? Two point seven tons! Even a force-twelve wind can’t budge it! Your dad’s driving and this car together are rock solid. Relax!”
The Maybach sped along the empty elevated road, throwing up sprays of water as tall as a person. The man turned on the stereo without asking and played “Daily Growing” by the Irish band Altan:
The trees they grow high, the leaves they do grow green,
Many is the time my true love I've seen,
Many an hour I have watched him all alone,
He’s young but he's daily growing.
Father, dear father, you've done me great wrong,
You have married me to a boy who is too young,
I am twice twelve and he is but fourteen,
He's young but he's daily growing.
“Good, isn’t it? Everyone said it was a great disc, so I bought it. It’s about a father’s love!” the man said.
Chu Zihang didn’t know whether to laugh or cry. “Can’t you hear? It’s a conversation between a girl and her father, not a boy. It’s not appropriate for me.”

“Boy or girl, what’s the difference? It’s a father’s love either way.” The man waved it off. “You understand it? I hear your English is top-notch at school, that you won a competition... But your mother never told me. What’s the song about?”

“A father marries his twenty-four-year-old daughter to a rich fourteen-year-old boy. She doesn’t want to; she worries she’ll be old by the time her husband grows up. But her father says his arrangement is right. He’s married her to a wealthy young man, so she’ll have someone to rely on when he’s old,” Chu Zihang said. “Later the boy dies before he grows up. The girl grieves terribly and weaves him a flannel shroud in a green graveyard.”

“What the hell kind of song is that? No fun at all. The girl’s husband dies before he even does anything?” The man really was not a sensitive creature. Chu Zihang had known since childhood that his biological father was as rough as they came.

“Let’s just have a chat, father and son.” The man turned off the stereo. “Did I tell you about our company’s new building? The boss put in a steam room and gym, free for us to use. Everything in there is so damn fancy...”
The man had failed in life because he talked too much... yet if he hadn’t talked so much, he might have failed even worse, Chu Zihang thought.

His gift of gab was how he had charmed Mom until she married beneath her. Everyone at Shilan High agreed Chu Zihang was handsome enough to live off his looks, thanks to his mother’s genes. In her youth she had been the star of the city dance troupe, dancing Silk Road Flower Rain like a flying apsara from a mural, with suitors as numerous as fish crossing a river. Somehow this man had fought his way through the field. Every day he drove to the troupe’s gate to pick her up after work, using nothing but his mouth to weave a beautiful future and charm her senseless. On a drive to Hangzhou she had absentmindedly agreed to marry beneath her, and on that same trip had conceived Chu Zihang. Only after pressing her fingerprints onto the marriage certificate did she learn the car wasn’t his: he was a driver for his work unit.

His politics teacher was right: the economic base determines the superstructure. A man like that couldn’t support the superstructure of a beautiful wife. His mother had always been absentminded and wasn’t greedy; the man was simply too hopeless.
And so, snap, it fell apart.

At the divorce, the man thumped his chest and promised his former wife he would earn money every month to support her and their son, show her he could make something of himself, and come back to propose once he had succeeded. Full of grand ambition, he promptly quit his stable job at the state enterprise to find more profitable work. After hanging around the labor market for three or four months without a single offer, he finally realized all he knew was driving. Shamefaced, he found a driving job at a private company. The boss of the Black Prince Group liked his gift of gab and put him behind the wheel of the Maybach. A driver needed to talk smoothly, so the boss could leave him to boast about things the boss couldn’t conveniently boast about himself.
The car was better than before, but his pay had hardly changed. After his own expenses, he couldn’t even support a cat.

Fortunately, Chu Zihang’s beautiful mother finally did something for herself. She had no intention of waiting for him. After several tearful days, she left Chu Zihang at his grandmother’s, bought new cosmetics, put on alluring makeup, and went barhopping with her friends. In less than a month, she brought Chu Zihang a new dad. Having learned from experience, she chose carefully this time: a man one in a thousand. “Dad” owned three companies, was divorced once, and had no children. When he proposed, he swore he would never have children of his own and would raise Chu Zihang as his son.

With a rich dad and beautiful mom, talented and capable himself, Chu Zihang seemed exceptionally fortunate to his classmates. They had no idea his private life was far more exceptional than they imagined. But he couldn’t take credit for it; his biological parents were the exceptional ones.
“Want to watch a DVD? I’ve got Shrek 2, though it’s a bootleg filmed in a theater.” The man stopped chattering, perhaps embarrassed at getting no response.
“No.” Chu Zihang hesitated. “The three of us are going to see it this weekend.”
The three meant Chu Zihang and his rich dad and beautiful mom. The man had nothing to do with it.

That was “Dad’s” rule. Busy with work, “Dad” gave his clients every meal from breakfast to late-night snacks. But after one divorce, he had recognized the importance of family, so he permanently marked one weekend day on his schedule for them. Their usual activities were shopping, a movie, and a lavish dinner, followed by a discussion of Chu Zihang’s studies. “Dad” followed his schedule strictly: never one day less or one day more of family time, just as he appeared in the company’s main conference room at nine every Monday, rain or shine, for the weekly meeting with senior executives.
How did a stepson with a face that rarely smiled deserve the same treatment as executives earning a million a year? It was all thanks to Mom.
“Is the air warm enough in back?” the man asked again.
“Enough. Stop talking like a chauffeur!” Chu Zihang was irritated.
You’re my father! Do you understand? he wanted to ask the man. Do you?

Under the visitation agreement you only get one day a month, and even then you’re often too busy. Even when you come, what can you say to me while you sit in someone else’s house? Actually, of course, you can talk plenty: you sit on the horsehair sofa “Dad” bought for 170,000 yuan and praise how fancy it is! Why did I ask you to pick me up? Because no one else would? Because if you picked me up, we could talk! If you can’t say anything profound, just ask plainly, casually, how I’ve been, whether I’m happy... Don’t hold an umbrella over me, so attentive. I don’t care about that. Do you want to kneel and change my rain boots like Liu Miaomiao’s driver? I don’t need a chauffeur. We already have one at home... You’re my father. Do you understand?
“What’s shameful about being my son’s chauffeur?” The man shrugged. His skin was as thick as a city wall, or his nerves slower than a turtle’s. “When you were little, you rode me like a horse.”
Something in Chu Zihang’s heart twitched, as though it had cracked and released bitter water. He was tired and didn’t want to speak. He leaned back against the leather seat and stared out the window.
He always said things that hurt so calmly... Couldn’t he stop bringing them up?

Many years ago... in that shabby little room of barely a dozen square meters, the man crawled around while a boy rode on his shoulders shouting “Giddyap!” and a beautiful woman fussed over the gas stove... The images flickered in his mind like a film played by a battered hand-cranked projector.
The sky slowly darkened and the streetlights came on. Through the layers of rain, their light was as faint as fireflies.
“How’s your mother lately?” the man asked, breaking the silence.

“Same as before. She gets up in the morning and plays with the cat, shops in the afternoon, and goes drinking with her friends at night. When they’re having fun they come back together and talk until late, then sleep until noon. Anyway...” Chu Zihang hesitated. “Dad is always out entertaining clients and has no time for her. He thinks it’s good that she amuses herself.”
The words were a little hurtful. A down-on-his-luck man asked after the woman he had once loved, and she was happy, having forgotten him altogether.

Grandma said Mom had been a carefree girl since childhood, but being carefree and beautiful meant she could live well. Mom had long since put her unhappiness behind her. She regarded “Dad” as her first husband: married happily in their youth, with an outstanding son like Chu Zihang. In Chinese, perfect; in English, perfect.
People had to accept reality. The man’s image had been erased from the limited memory in Mom’s head.

Calling another man “Dad” in front of him was not easy for Chu Zihang either. A moment ago he had tactfully said “the three of us.” But once the word was out, it wasn’t so awkward. He had promised “Dad” to call him Dad, not Uncle, Four-Eyes, or Side Parting... even though in Chu Zihang’s mind “Dad” was a four-eyed fellow with a side part, or a side-parted fellow with glasses. But Chu Zihang was stubborn about keeping promises, whether people were watching or not.
After all these years, surely the man was used to it. He hadn’t tried hard to win custody of his son back then, anyway.
“Take good care of your mother,” the man said.
In the rearview mirror, his still handsome but somewhat aging face showed little expression.
“Mm. Like you said, I make sure she drinks milk before bed. If she’s talking with her friends, I warm it and bring it to her.”

It was the only thing the man had asked Chu Zihang to do. Strange: he had lost the woman, yet still remembered a cup of milk. Since childhood Mom had needed a glass of warm milk with half a spoonful of sugar every night, so she wouldn’t wake repeatedly. By now she had probably forgotten that years ago the man had warmed it for her. Before him, Grandma had done it; after him, her son did.
A fortunate woman always had someone to warm her milk.
“Shilan High is damn impressive! Seventeen students got into Tsinghua and Peking University this year. Work hard, son! Don’t disgrace me!” The man made a show of concern for Chu Zihang’s studies.
“Dad says I’m not taking the domestic entrance exam. I’m going abroad for college. I’m taking the TOEFL next month,” Chu Zihang replied coldly.
Disgrace him? When had he ever really cared? He only ever talked.
Last year a coproduced movie had filmed locally, and Chu Zihang had been chosen as an extra. Hearing about it, the man had sworn he would visit the set.
“My son’s making a movie! I’ll bring tea and water. If I drive this car there, I’ll look spectacular, won’t I?” He patted the wheel, beaming.

So during breaks Chu Zihang kept looking, consciously or not, toward the parking lot. The spectacular Maybach never appeared. But “Dad’s” Mercedes S500 was always there, with the driver, Old Shun, wearing huge dark glasses and a neck thicker than a man’s head, looking every bit a bodyguard. He called Chu Zihang “young master” in front of everyone and behind their backs, making people stare.

And then there was that disastrous middle-school entrance ceremony. It fell on “Dad” and Mom’s wedding anniversary, when they were going on vacation to northern Europe. After much thought, Chu Zihang called the man and asked him to come. The man was happy but hesitant: what about your mother and stepfather? After a long silence Chu Zihang said, just say you’re my uncle. The man didn’t feel slighted at all. He chuckled and said, then remember to call me Uncle; don’t let it slip... In the end Chu Zihang was the only student with no parent standing behind him at the ceremony. He stood in the most prominent place, first in line, as the principal awarded him the new-student scholarship. He ranked first among Shilan’s incoming class and had wanted to surprise the man.

“Oh, I really didn’t forget, but that day the boss suddenly said an important client was coming and wanted a bath, so I had to drive them there. Who knew they’d bathe until the next morning...” Later the man scratched his head and mumbled his explanation.
Chu Zihang had a vague idea what sort of person the man’s “boss” was, and what sort of place he meant by “a bath.”
A classmate had told Chu Zihang, “I saw your Maybach parked outside a bathhouse last time,” then lowered his voice. “Isn’t that a place where people do bad things?”

Obviously. At the entrance, decorated like a Roman palace, seven or eight heavily made-up hostesses wore skirts almost short enough to reach their waists and necklines nearly low enough to fall below their breasts. Men of every kind climbed out of luxury cars and marched in, bellies thrust forward. Chu Zihang had passed once and glanced from a distance, imagining the man’s boss and clients reveling inside at night while the man leaned against his beloved Maybach, smoking, the smoke spreading into the dark.
Chu Zihang didn’t blame him much. The man was simply who he was and lived the life he lived, very far removed from Chu Zihang’s.

“Going abroad isn’t good,” the man mumbled. “It’s not fashionable anymore. China’s developing so fast; opportunities are everywhere. If you ask me, go to college here, study finance, and have your stepdad use his connections to find you a job...”
It was as though a needle pierced Chu Zihang’s chest. He shuddered with pain. “Have your stepdad use his connections”... Couldn’t a person have some dignity? Did he have to be so shameless?
“Shut up!” Chu Zihang growled.
“What?” The man hadn’t heard clearly.
“Shut up.” Chu Zihang was like a young lion with its fur on end.
“What a rude child. I’m doing this for your own good.” The man stared. “You should listen to adults...”

“Is listening to you any use? If I listen to you, will I find a girl and marry her without getting divorced? Will I make it to my son’s graduation on time? Will I pick him up and drop him off at school on time? If I listen to you, all I’ll do is ask my stepfather to use his connections!” Chu Zihang stared into the man’s eyes in the rearview mirror, hoping to see disappointment or anger.
Every word struck at the heart.

Many people thought Chu Zihang couldn’t even swear, much less speak with cutting bitterness. Even when fouled on the basketball court he never lost his temper, only raised a hand for the referee. But who couldn’t say cruel things, when anger lay buried like needles in the heart? Now he was furious and wanted to stab the man hard with those needles. The words came out without thought.

“You’re still young. Family matters... you’ll understand when you’re older.” The man was clearly at a loss. He reached out as if to pat Chu Zihang in the back seat, but didn’t dare; he drew his hand back and scratched his head.

It was always the same answer: “You’ll understand later,” “You’re too young,” “It’s not what you think.” Bullshit! When those two fools divorced, Chu Zihang had been small. He had cried as though the world were ending, and the man comforted him with “It’s not what you think,” “Mom and Dad just won’t live together,” “I’ll still take you out on Sundays.” Chu Zihang believed him; he believed home was still the three of them. Then he followed Mom into their new house and saw a gentleman with side-parted hair, a bathrobe, and two hairy legs politely open the door. Not knowing who this stranger was, Chu Zihang was so shocked that he shoved his ice cream into the man’s face.
All these years later, the little kid had grown up, and they were still lying? To hell with that!
“Enough! Just drive, and stay out of my business! When we get home, don’t come in. ‘Dad’ might be unhappy!” Chu Zihang clenched his teeth and turned away.
“What kind of thing is that to say? I’m your real father. If he’s unhappy, let him be unhappy. Who the hell is he...” At last the man sounded wounded in his pride.

“He isn’t my real father, but he comes to parent-teacher meetings. He takes me to amusement parks on weekends. He knows my final grades. At least he buys me a schoolbag for my birthday!” Chu Zihang slammed the Hermès bag against the seat. “Do you even remember my birthday?”

“Of course I remember!” the man protested, red-faced. “You’re my son. Your mom and I made you together... As soon as we heard she was pregnant, we counted the days, when you were conceived and when you were due, waiting eagerly. You little rascal wouldn’t come out; you stayed two months extra! How could I forget? Haven’t you had health class? Men deserve credit for making babies too. Aren’t you smart because I made you well?”
Chu Zihang was so angry he nearly laughed. How could any man be so shameless?

“Was it hard? Marrying a beautiful woman and having her give birth... was that such an achievement?” His voice shook. “I’ve had health class! The woman carries the baby for ten difficult months. What does the man do? What was hard for you?”
The man wilted, his voice sinking. “I’m not discussing health class with my son...”

“Was it hard after I was born? Did you ever look after me? Why exactly are you my ‘real father’? Just because you and Mom ‘made me together’? As though you manufactured some product? Tell me what ‘real father’ actually means.” Chu Zihang’s mood was as bad as it could get, and the anger he had suppressed flared again.

“A real father means... you... carry my blood.” The man chose his words carefully. “You’re my legacy in this world, don’t you understand? You’re half of me... I know I haven’t looked after you much these years, and I’m sorry, but what father doesn’t care about his child? Our blood connects us, we...”
“Live and prosper together, too!” Chu Zihang sneered.

The man fell silent, and so did Chu Zihang. Only thousands upon thousands of raindrops drummed heavily on the roof. The air inside seemed to grow much colder all at once, beyond the reach of the heater.

After a long time the man sighed slowly, sounding like he was repeating an old saying. “That’s why I say you’re young. You don’t understand. When you have a child of your own, you’ll see. Having a child is like giving half of yourself to that child. It’s as if you can sense where he is, like telepathy. You’ll always care about him and think about him. It comes naturally, for no reason at all. Besides, everyone dies. When I die, everyone else will forget me, but you’ll still be in this world, and half of you is me. It’s as though I’ve left something behind.”
“You only know how to make a child, not raise one. If someone else raises him, he’ll grow less and less like you!”
“I... I wanted to raise you too,” the man said haltingly.

A low laugh came from the stereo. Chu Zihang started, unsure whether it was static or the CD player accidentally turning on. The laughter was deep, immense and solemn, as though echoing inside an ancient bronze bell. He had been watching the man’s face in the rearview mirror. Suddenly it changed: blue veins sprang up at the corners of his eyes like restless little snakes. His usually slack face tightened, like red-hot iron quenched in ice water.
Chu Zihang had never seen that expression on him. He was a different person altogether, his abruptly narrowed pupils betraying immense terror.
Someone tapped softly on the car door.
“In rain this heavy, who’s outside?” Chu Zihang turned and saw a black shadow cast on the window. Had the elevated road been closed, and traffic police come to check? He reached to lower the window.
“Sit back!” the man barked.
A vast terror suddenly engulfed Chu Zihang. He glanced at the speedometer: 120 kilometers an hour. Who could run after the Maybach on the elevated road and reach out to knock at the same time?

The knocking grew urgent. There was not one figure but three, five, more and more gathering outside, staring down at Chu Zihang through the rain-streaked windows. A dazzling mercury-colored light shone from outside, turning both their faces deathly pale. The man turned to Chu Zihang and struggled to keep his voice from shaking. “Don’t be afraid... son!”
The knocking became the piercing scrape of sharp things across steel and glass. Chu Zihang thought they must be the shadows’ nails.
“Where are we?” he screamed.
The man reached back, seized his wrist, hauled him bodily from the back seat, and threw him into the passenger seat.
“Buckle up!” he said quietly. All fear had vanished from his face, which was hard as cast iron.

He floored the accelerator. The Maybach shuddered and surged forward. Within seconds it reached 180 kilometers an hour and continued accelerating, because they had failed to shake the shadows. Mercury-colored light came from every direction, revealing countless dark figures surrounding the car... standing silently... like a crowd of death gods around a dying person’s bed. They opened their eyes together, golden pupils blazing like torches. Chu Zihang curled up, clutching his head in pain.

Pain tore through the depths of his brain. Tangled blue-violet lines twisted like countless snakes, like hieroglyphs on an ancient tablet come alive and dancing like spirits. Images he would never have dared imagine in his worst nightmares flashed before him: a young man with a golden eye split open in his forehead lay on a black stone throne, a long bone sword in his chest; girls writhed on a carved stone altar, screaming in pain as if labor were beginning; black wings rose against the sunset, blotting out half the sky; a woman bound to a bronze pillar slowly opened her eyes, white hair flying as two streams of foul blood ran down her face...
It was like watching snakes dance in the primeval darkness, telling him a lost history in a strange language.

“It’s spirit vision. Your bloodline is being awakened. Such a strong reaction—I don’t know whether it’s your luck... or your misfortune.” The man gripped Chu Zihang’s hand. “I always hoped this day... would come later.”

After an unknown time, Chu Zihang slowly lifted his head, as if waking from a nightmare as long as a lifetime. The feeling was hard to describe: like a nearsighted man putting on glasses after years without them, the world suddenly became extraordinarily clear. Sight, hearing, even smell awoke. He looked blankly at the man, who gently stroked his head, in a gesture that might have been care or sorrow.
“What’s happening? Are we going to die?” Chu Zihang asked.
“Son, welcome to”—the man drew a deep breath—“the real world.”
“The real... world?”

“Don’t tell anyone what you just saw, or whatever you see next. No one will believe you; they’ll think you’re crazy,” the man said. “I think living in an unreal world is happier, so I always wanted you to learn all this later. I kept trying to stay away from you so I wouldn’t drag you into it. But when I got your text today... I couldn’t stop myself from picking you up... Well, it’s no big deal. If a father wants to make an impression on his son, he has to act like a man. I never had the chance before.” He licked his lips. “Are these guys giving me a stage to show off? Not bad!”
Chu Zihang didn’t understand. He thought the man must have been scared out of his wits. Why was he talking nonsense?

The Maybach had reached its top speed, 275 kilometers an hour, the tachometer needle jumping into the dangerous red zone. The man floored the accelerator, gripped the wheel, and stared ahead. There was only mercury-colored light; nothing was visible, as though they were racing toward a silver sea. Pale handprints without palm lines struck the windshield with loud bangs. Shadows pounded the windows on every side, hard enough to break blast-resistant glass.
The man pulled the black umbrella from the door.

Was he going to get out and talk to the shadows with an umbrella at a time like this? Chu Zihang stared, then saw clearly: it wasn’t an umbrella but a sword, a slender Japanese blade in a black sheath, with no guard. It was a devotional sword. Chu Zihang had read a book called Knowledge of Japanese Swords: in Japan, swordsmiths omitted the guard only on two kinds of sword, those carried by poor ronin and ceremonial swords dedicated to the gods. Sacred swords were never used for cutting, so a guard was unnecessary. The sword’s elegant, antique-style sharkskin sheath showed it was a decorative craft object.
The blade slipped from the sheath, its gleam clear as water.

Chu Zihang was dumbfounded. What was happening? Wasn’t the man a driver, a loser who should be carefully ferrying his boss around? Yet now he held the sword, eager to act, radiating an edge sharp as a spear... with a decorative sword?

“Sacred sword Murasame, the cursed blade destined to kill the Tokugawa family. Heard of it?” The man laid it across the steering wheel. “The original was destroyed long ago. They recast it in regenerated metal and enshrined it at Gion Shrine for ten years.”

Veins bulged on the man’s wrist. Reversing his grip, he thrust straight into the left door. The long blade pierced the cast-aluminum door and lodged there, half its length exposed outside. He slammed on the brakes. The speedometer plunged, the wheels skidding on the verge of losing control. Foul blood trailed a black ribbon a dozen meters long in the wind, then the rain washed it away. The shadows couldn’t slow in time; those on the left were cut through by the exposed blade before they could even cry out. Simple, pure killing, as though they had struck its sharp edge at 250 kilometers an hour. Black blood splashed across every window on the left and even seeped through the cracks. Chu Zihang held his head and trembled uncontrollably.

Sacred sword Murasame—was it a decorative replica? It had been forged to kill! Its tough blade could cut through the bones of more than a dozen people without breaking. This way of killing... this man, and the whole world... had they all gone mad?

The man immediately floored the accelerator. Tires shrieked against the road: wheelspin, the power exceeding their grip. Even through the air filter came the smell of burning rubber. He jerked the wheel and the Maybach spun out, its heavy 2.7-ton body sweeping the shadows away and into the roadside barrier, which cracked under the impacts.
Black blood coated all the windows, only to be washed away by the rain.
It was hell.

As the car spun violently, the man pressed a warm palm to Chu Zihang’s head. Chu Zihang suddenly remembered childhood, when the man, the woman, and he were still a family, and the man took him to ride a carousel, holding his head just as gently.

The car stopped, facing the opposite direction. The man floored it again, and the Maybach charged back the way they had come like an enraged stallion. A chilling sound came from under the wheels, like bones being crushed... The car kept shuddering as one shadow after another flew away. The man held the accelerator down, his face expressionless. In his hands the car had become a killing machine. Chu Zihang couldn’t believe such a useless man had suddenly become a demon who killed without blinking.
“Don’t be afraid. Things like Deadpool... don’t have civil rights,” the man said hoarsely. “They aren’t human, so the law doesn’t protect them!”

One shadow wasn’t thrown aside. Taller than the others, he was built like a giant. He braced both hands against the hood and was driven rapidly backward by the Maybach, his feet scraping shrilly against the road. In the rain his golden eyes seemed to burn. The scene belonged in a Superman or Spider-Man movie. For an ordinary person, such enormous friction would dislocate joints and break leg bones.

“Die!” the man growled. The Maybach drove the shadow into the barrier. He shifted into reverse, then forward, accelerated, and struck again, then a third and fourth time, until the barrier broke. Only then did the gold in the shadow’s eyes dim like a lamp out of oil. Even so, he made no sound.

The man turned the car and accelerated away. Trembling, Chu Zihang looked through the rear window. The fallen shadows slowly rose, their golden eyes flickering as they silently watched the car recede.
“Those... who are they? Call... call 110!” Chu Zihang looked fearfully at the man.
“No use. Your phone probably has no signal,” the man said softly.
“As for who they are... that would take some explaining,” he added after a moment.
“Don’t be afraid, son. A dad for one day is a dad for life. Your dad’s still your dad, not a monster.” One glance at Chu Zihang told him what the terror in his son’s eyes meant.
“Don’t worry, don’t worry. Your dad is actually very capable. I just don’t look the part...”

Apparently he was still the same man; at least he was just as talkative. But Chu Zihang could see he was far from relaxed. Sweat covered his face, his hands trembled slightly on the wheel, and he hunched like a shrimp, eyes fixed on the road ahead.

Sure enough, the phone had no signal. Chu Zihang turned on the radio; only static came through. GPS couldn’t find a satellite signal either. Everything was beyond his understanding. How could so many strange people be on an elevated highway? It was covered in surveillance cameras, yet no road police came after such a serious accident. They seemed to have entered a space cut off from the world, containing only the elevated road, the storm, the shadows, and the Maybach.
“To put it simply, your bloodline is a little different from other people’s.” After a long silence, the man offered this rather unconvincing explanation.
“Don’t look like it’s the end of the world. A different bloodline is nothing to be ashamed of. Mine’s different too. If you hadn’t inherited it from me, you’d be perfectly normal.”

He scratched his head. “Forget it. Let’s not talk about it now. I’ll explain properly when there’s time... Actually, going abroad isn’t bad. But remember, don’t apply to a college called Cassell. It’s full of lunatics.”
“Say, will your stepdad leave you his fortune? Keep an eye on him. Don’t let him take a mistress... or there’ll be someone competing with you for the inheritance,” the man said seriously.
“Have you seen Indiana Jones? The professor and his son are great! My lifelong dream is just like that: Dad driving in front, son behind him firing a machine gun!”
What went on inside this man’s head? Even now he could chatter and grow animated.

They raced on for more than ten minutes. At their speed they had covered over forty kilometers. The shadows hadn’t caught up, and the mercury light had vanished. Chu Zihang’s pounding heart slowly returned to normal. Surely nothing in the world could run as fast as a Maybach at top speed. They should have left the shadows forty kilometers behind.
“Where are we going now?” he asked.
“I don’t know. They’re still here... they haven’t gone... because the rain hasn’t stopped. We have to find the exit.” The man kept the accelerator floored. Chu Zihang could see he was no less tense.
The rain hadn’t stopped? What did that mean? What did rain have to do with the shadows? His head was splitting.
A speed-reduction sign flashed past, announcing a toll station one kilometer ahead. Bright white lights emerged from the darkness. The man let out a long breath of relief.

“We should be back in a normal area. Get out after the toll station and see if a passing car can take you home. Your dad can give them some money.” The man took out several banknotes for the toll, then pulled the sword from the car door.
“Where are you going?” Chu Zihang asked.
“They’ll follow me. Don’t worry, your dad really is capable, and this car—a nine-million-yuan Maybach—is no joke. I can outrun them.”
At a time like this, he was still boasting about his car? Chu Zihang looked at him speechlessly.
“I was joking. Don’t take it seriously.” The man smiled. “But I really will be fine. I still have to attend your parent-teacher meetings. Don’t worry... son.”

The Maybach didn’t slow. The toll station drew closer, its brilliant white light warm as an inn’s lamp seen beneath the eaves by a traveler lost in night fog, making him quicken his steps, knowing he could lay down his worries once he arrived. Both Chu Zihang and the man gazed eagerly ahead.
The car abruptly slowed, brake pads squealing.
“No... something’s wrong!” the man said hoarsely.
Chu Zihang sensed it too. The light ahead conveyed not only warmth but solemnity and grandeur, like... pilgrims approaching a temple.
Yes! That longing to draw near wasn’t like seeing a lighthouse at sea. It was the reverent desire to worship a god, to approach the radiance of divinity.
But Chu Zihang believed in no god, none at all... until he saw that light.
They had stopped, but the light came toward them, threads of white radiating through darkness and rain.

Chu Zihang heard a horse neigh. He thought it must be an illusion. It sounded very much like a horse, but if it really was, what an immense creature it must be! Its deep roar was like thunder held in its mouth, lightning shooting from its nostrils.
“Listen to your dad. Don’t get too far away from me, but don’t get too close either.” The man looked at him. “Like when I took you to fly a kite.”
A kite never strays far from the person flying it, because a string connects them. When it does fly away, the string has broken.
Chu Zihang nodded.
“Buckle your seat belt!” The man pressed the accelerator with all his strength.
The Maybach surged forward at maximum acceleration, charging straight into the white light. The mist parted, and Chu Zihang suddenly saw what stood in the radiance...
His worldview collapsed. Everything he had believed was shattered. The world was nothing like he had imagined!

In the white light stood a horse as mighty as a mountain, draped in heavy armor inlaid with metal patterns, its white coat glowing like crystal. Eight powerful legs resembled the outriggers that steady a wheeled crane. Dark-gold horseshoes tore one wound after another in the hard road. A mask covered its face, and after each thunderous neigh, sparks of lightning sprayed from its metal nostrils.

A huge black figure sat astride it, encased in heavy dark-gold armor that glimmered under the rain. He carried a curved spear, its shaft arcing like a meteor across the sky. Behind his iron mask, a single golden eye lit the surroundings like a great lamp.
Odin, chief god of the Norse Aesir!

Chu Zihang had read his story in a book. Now he had come, just as in legend: riding the eight-legged Sleipnir, carrying Gungnir, a spear made from a branch of the World Tree, clad in dark-gold armor and a dark-blue cloak, one-eyed!
He should have existed only in words and murals!

The Maybach crashed into him. Sleipnir screamed, four front hooves rearing into the air. Rain from every direction gathered before Odin and struck the front of the Maybach. Chu Zihang could see nothing; it was as though a waterfall rushed toward them. The car’s immense momentum dissolved within a few meters. Alarms sounded and airbags deployed, saving Chu Zihang’s neck from snapping instantly.

The torrent pushed the Maybach back. Sleipnir slowly sank to its eight knees and stopped. Odin drove Gungnir into the wet asphalt, his divine horse his throne. Crowds of black figures emerged behind him like priests preparing for Mass. They surrounded the car on every side, all in identical black clothes, with identical pale faces and identical hollow eyes shining gold. The Maybach was completely surrounded. Apparently the gods’ tactics resembled those of humans.
“Get out,” the man said softly.
Chu Zihang moved mechanically, following him out. They stood side by side in the brilliant headlights, the man holding the long sword in one hand and drawing Chu Zihang close with the other.
“Don’t be afraid... although I was terrified the first time I saw it too... But fear won’t help. I didn’t want you to see this, but since you have, don’t miss the chance. Open your eyes wide!”

Chu Zihang gripped his hand. He had never felt the man so tall, as immovable as a mountain. Rain filled heaven and earth; beyond it lay limitless darkness. Beneath them stretched the broad elevated road, surrounded by transparent curtains of water, as though all the world’s rain had gathered in this space, streams pressed together without gaps.
“You dare crash into the throne of a god!” Odin’s deep voice came through the rain.
“I’m a driver. When you drive too much, your hand inevitably slips.” The man spoke calmly. “I know what you want. Fine, I can give it to you.”
He patted Chu Zihang’s head. “Get the case from the trunk. Black, with a silver emblem.”
There was indeed a black case in the trunk, its special leather rough and tough, with a silver plate engraved with a flourishing World Tree.
Chu Zihang handed it to the man, who weighed it, gave it back, and looked at Odin. “I’m ready.”
“Then, human! Approach!”

“You’ve disobeyed me many times, but this time you must listen,” the man whispered in Chu Zihang’s ear. “Remember, don’t leave me, but don’t get too close. When I say ‘run,’ run toward the car. Don’t look back, whatever you do. Don’t look back!”
“Mm!” Chu Zihang trembled.

The shadows closed around them and carried them forward, whispering to one another in an ancient tongue, like singing and weeping. Chu Zihang couldn’t understand a word, but the snakelike lines in his mind were waking, shifting endlessly. Suddenly he understood those eager voices of the dead:
“Human...”
“Humans again...”
“The child’s bloodline...”
“Such mouthwatering fresh meat...”
“Thirsty...”
Chu Zihang covered his ears and looked around in terror. The shadows’ faces were all alike, all expressionless, yet each bore too many stories of the past.
“I hear what you hear. Don’t be afraid. Dad is beside you,” the man whispered.
The man stopped about a hundred meters from Odin and a hundred from the Maybach behind them, exactly halfway between. Rain washed continuously over the sword in his hand.
“Even if I give you the thing, I don’t think you’ll let us go,” he said.
He planted his feet wide, soaked trousers flapping in the cold wind, looking as swaggering as a street thug. But showing a thug’s swagger before something like a god?
“I will promise you life,” Odin said. “A god never lies to mortals.”
“Life like these dead men?” The man pointed his thumb at the shadows.
“No. Your bloodlines are far superior to theirs. You will be much stronger.”
“No room to bargain?”
“All who have been to this realm can return to it. Therefore everyone who comes here must be a servant of god.”
“Son, they say you’re a center on the city team, good at breaking through defenses?” the man murmured in Chu Zihang’s ear.
Chu Zihang nodded nervously.
“Negotiations have broken down,” the man said. “Give me the case.”
He took it and gently stroked Chu Zihang’s head. “Remember everything I told you. Every word.” He suddenly slapped Chu Zihang on the rear and roared, “Run!”

Without thinking, Chu Zihang turned and ran madly toward the car. For a long time he had no longer believed the man’s words, but on this rainy night, holding his warm hand, he had suddenly become a child dependent on his father again.

The man hurled the case toward Odin, like fresh meat thrown to draw wolves. Half the shadows rushed after it, half intercepted the man and Chu Zihang. Their forms distorted with speed, like long snakes springing from the ground. The man ran after Chu Zihang, but perhaps because he was middle-aged, he wasn’t as fast; the distance between them widened. Watching his son’s back recede, a smile touched his mouth. “Fast little rascal.”
He spun, his sword carving a blinding arc and sending rain splashing outward in a circle.
Chu Zihang heard terrible sounds pursuing him: blood pouring from wounds, bones breaking beneath a blade, mingled with the storm.
He actually heard the shadows wailing: “It hurts,” “It hurts so much,” “It burns with pain”... desperate cries, as if from hell.

Thick, foul blood without warmth spattered his back, and even the rain could not wash it away. The man remained behind him. Chu Zihang gathered his courage and looked back. Like a lion the man swung his sword, and shadow after shadow split in its gleam.
A transparent curtain of air opened in the rain. A high cry burst from deep in the man’s throat, as ancient as the shadows’ whispers.

Where the curtain spread, time slowed. Wind and rain seemed to thicken, and the shadows slowed too, everything like a film in slow motion. Only the man was unaffected. He turned and swung his sword, stepping and sliding, water slowly splashing underfoot and the shadows’ foul black blood slowly flowing out, all suspended for a moment in the air like ink drifting through water. Amid the ink, his flashing blade was a silver swallow in flight.
Chu Zihang had never imagined a man could look so magnificent, and this man was his father.
At last he threw himself into the car and shouted into the rain, “Dad!”
Suddenly he had a strange feeling... the kite string had broken.
It was the string between him and the man. For a very long time he had seen him only at long intervals, but there had always been a string between them. Now it had broken.
The man had not run back with him. After shaking off the shadows, he had turned and raced toward Odin!

The shadows with the case had counterattacked, and the man’s domain expanded to cover them all. But Odin did not slow. He drew Gungnir and struck, lightning darting. Countless thrusts in an instant: each stroke of the legendary spear that always found its mark carried a dark-gold gleam. Arcs of light surrounded the man, attacking vital points from different directions like a dense meteor shower.
The man ignored the shadows. He dodged among the meteors, spinning with his sword, stepping on a shadow to leap high, and struck downward—at Odin, at the god’s head!

Blood suddenly poured from his back. He fell among the shadows. The “meteors” he had dodged curved around like fireflies and struck him from behind. Odin withdrew Gungnir, and the shadows closed on the man step by step.
“Son! Drive away!” He turned sharply and roared at Chu Zihang, thick blood-red mist rising from his body.
Chu Zihang understood. The man wanted to draw every shadow surrounding them to himself. He was using himself as bait.

“Listen to me! Remember what you promised.” The man’s blood-red eyes stayed fixed on Odin, but he spoke to Chu Zihang. “If I die, you’re all I leave in this world. If you die too, I’ll have nothing left here.”
“Son, trust your dad. If you live, we’ll have a chance to meet again.” He flexed his bleeding arm. “With you here, there are some of my big moves I can’t use.”
“That car’s wonderful. It cost nine million! Something that damn expensive can’t be stopped even by a god!”
Chu Zihang looked at the keyless console. He understood what the man had boasted about: three people could awaken the engine, and he was the third.
“Start,” he said.
The engine roared.
“Well done, son!” The man raised his sword, his voice like thunder.
Chu Zihang reversed, the car flying backward. The man had secretly taught him to drive in this very Maybach; they had once sped along a country dirt road in spring with the sunroof open.

The Maybach struck a barely visible curtain of rain. Whirling wind battered its body, walls of water pressed in from every side. The twelve-cylinder engine roared at full power, but could not move the car out of that place.
“Hey! God! Open sesame!” the man roared, hurling his sword at the eight-legged horse’s head. Gungnir struck again. The man leaped, surrounded by countless golden meteors.
The water wall’s force weakened for an instant. The Maybach roared through it and plunged into the deep night.
Chu Zihang’s mind was blank. He drove mechanically through the rain. At some point the stereo had come on again, and daughter and father were singing to each other:
Daughter, dear daughter, the match I made was right,
I married you to a wealthy family’s son,
When I grow old, he will be the man you can rely on,
He is young, but he is growing.
Suddenly he understood the song.

Those were the words the man wanted to leave him. Whether he was a son or daughter didn’t matter: the man had sent him into a wealthy family because he had no certainty about his own life. He wanted his child to live well and have someone to rely on.

This was a man who always lived a double life. Only rarely was he fierce and formidable; in most people’s eyes he was a man of little ability. Yet he dared not show that fierce side to his son, so he could appear only as a driver, snatching time to collect him from school. That was all he could do. Many times he had waited outside the school in the Maybach, only to see the Mercedes S500 arrive and retreat with his head lowered. Believing his “daughter” had someone to rely on, he fled far away.
“You’ll understand when you’re older.”
Now Chu Zihang understood. And the man... the man might already be dead.
What was death?
It was the end, a final parting, something irretrievable: a hand you could never hold again, warmth you could never feel, and “I’m sorry” you could never say.

Chu Zihang slammed on the brakes. Tires shrieked; the car stopped sideways on the empty elevated road in the rain. He opened the sunroof and leaned back, gasping like an asthmatic, looking up. It seemed all the world’s rain poured through the opening, hard and cold against his face, but he felt neither cold nor pain. Only the man’s voice and the song played back in his ears.
“Start! Start!” he suddenly shouted at the console.
The engine gave a low, feeble sound. The car had reached its limit and could not move again.

Chu Zihang flung open the door and ran into the wind and rain. At that instant he understood that he was truly about to lose the man. What the man would leave in the world, what he had promised him—all of it was forgotten. He had gone mad. He feared neither the shadows nor Odin nor Gungnir. He had to find the man.
In the downpour, a small figure sat on the Maybach’s roof and watched him go, eyes faintly golden, humming the Irish folk song.
On July 3, 2004, Typhoon Dandelion, number 0407, made landfall in the city, bringing torrential rain and force-ten winds. The city was given three days off.

For the people of this coastal city, typhoons were ordinary, so no one panicked. Instead they happily enjoyed three unexpected days at home. Unable to go out, families sat together watching variety shows on television, and parents took the opportunity to make up for the time they usually couldn’t spend with their children.

Naturally the typhoon caused trouble. Although the elevated road had been closed promptly, some drivers had still gone up. Eventually the wind grew too strong for them to drive, and police cars couldn’t reach them. Officers phoned and told them to park against the barrier, close their windows tightly, and endure the night in the storm. Thanks to this, no cars were overturned, though their paint was scraped against the barrier and water got into their engines. In the morning the wind subsided and tow trucks went up to bring them out one by one. Every rescued person was overjoyed. A damaged car was nothing; insurance would pay. Having escaped death, everything was wonderful. At the exit they embraced waiting relatives, young people kissed, and older men and women wept. What a moving scene.

At last the families waiting at the exit left one by one, until only a boy remained. Without an umbrella, soaked through, he stood behind the crowd watching every car towed down. He seemed frozen, lips purple, trembling slightly, yet he did not move. Finally, when all the tow trucks had assembled and were about to leave, he approached the officer in charge. “Are there no more?”

“No more,” the officer said. “Haven’t found your family? Don’t worry, we rescued everyone on the elevated road. Nobody was hurt. If you didn’t see them, you must have missed each other. Go home and check.”
Something faint in the boy’s eyes seemed finally to go out. After a long silence he slowly crouched, both hands on the ground, saying nothing.

The officer couldn’t see his face and thought he was crying. He wanted to pat his shoulder and comfort him. A boy didn’t need to cry just because something had gone wrong; when in trouble, ask the police...

But he suddenly stopped. He did not dare approach. He could clearly see the boy’s ten fingers, braced against the ground and curled into claws, digging deep into the asphalt. He had no time to wonder how a middle-school boy possessed such terrifying strength. He simply sensed, instinctively, the overwhelming waves of... sorrow erupting from that slender body.
On the night of July 12, 2010, rain fell on the city again, a fine, steady drizzle.

The World Cup final in South Africa: Spain against the Netherlands. The streets were empty, traffic lights changing lonely colors. All over the city, people gathered before televisions, drinking beer and shouting at good plays and bad.

Chu Zihang lay on his back in the dark, hands folded on his chest, staring at the enameled chandelier. Mom and her friends screamed in the next room; someone must have scored. They had already finished a case of beer. If they kept drinking, those beautiful, eccentric aunties would run into the garden in low-cut silk nightgowns, holding hands and acting crazy. But never mind; let them. A little madness once in a while was fine.
Mom had already drunk her milk tonight.

Chu Zihang was reciting his diary. It was written neither on paper nor in an electronic file, but in his mind. It contained many images, passing frame by frame: riding on the man’s shoulders shouting “Giddyap!”; the only expensive toy the man had bought him, a model train set; and the scene the man himself would have considered the most spectacular of his life, standing with legs apart and holding a sword for worshiping—or killing—a god... Every night before sleep, Chu Zihang recalled them, every detail, until he was sure he had forgotten nothing.

Masashi Toyama, who taught Introduction to Brain Science, said human memory was unreliable, like a worn-out hard drive easily demagnetized. The past was like a picture drawn in sand. As time passed, wind blew the sand away, memory blurred, and finally everything became an indistinguishable haze. Toyama said this was a form of self-protection: imagine remembering every detail of the past forever. The saddest, most painful, most sorrowful images of your life would torment you constantly, and you could never escape the bad times behind you.
But Chu Zihang did not want to forget, because he was the only person in the world who still remembered that man. If he forgot too, it would be as though the man had never existed.
The man had once said that if he died one day, only one thing in the world could prove he had existed: Chu Zihang, who carried half his blood.
“Dad, it’s raining again.” Having recalled the final image, Chu Zihang spoke softly.
Rain rattled against the window. He slowly closed his eyes and fell asleep.
